questions.q: What is the order of the matrix A = [a_ij] where i = 1, 2, 3 and j = 1, 2, 3, 4? How many elements does it contain?
questions.a: The order is 3 × 4 (3 rows, 4 columns) and it contains 3 × 4 = 12 elements. A wrong answer like 4 × 3 or 7 elements reveals confusion between row/column indexing — the student is reading i as columns and j as rows, or adding m + n instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A student writes: "The matrix B = [5] is a row matrix because it has one row." Is this correct? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. The matrix [5] has order 1 × 1 — it is BOTH a row matrix (1 × n with n=1) AND a column matrix (m × 1 with m=1). It is also a square matrix, a diagonal matrix, a scalar matrix, and an identity matrix (since the single element is 1 if we consider [1]). A student who says it is "only a row matrix" does not understand that matrix types are not mutually exclusive; a 1 × 1 matrix satisfies all definitions simultaneously.

questions.q: Construct a 2 × 3 matrix A = [a_ij] where a_ij = (i - 2j)^2. Write the complete matrix with all elements calculated.
questions.a:
For i=1,2 and j=1,2,3:
a_11 = (1-2)^2 = 1, a_12 = (1-4)^2 = 9, a_13 = (1-6)^2 = 25
a_21 = (2-2)^2 = 0, a_22 = (2-4)^2 = 4, a_23 = (2-6)^2 = 16
Matrix A = [[1, 9, 25], [0, 4, 16]]. A wrong answer with elements like (1-2)^2 = -1 reveals sign error in squaring; an answer with 3 rows reveals order confusion (thinking 2×3 means 3 rows).

questions.q: Given matrices P = [[2, 0], [0, 2]] and Q = [[2, 0], [0, 3]], classify each as: diagonal, scalar, identity, or N/A. Justify your classification for each.
questions.a: P is diagonal (non-diagonal elements zero) AND scalar (diagonal elements equal, k=2) but NOT identity (diagonal elements not 1). Q is diagonal (non-diagonal elements zero) but NOT scalar (diagonal elements 2 and 3 are unequal) and NOT identity. A student who calls Q a scalar matrix is applying the "diagonal elements non-zero" condition but missing the "all diagonal elements equal" requirement.

questions.q: A student claims: "If A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[1, 2], [3, 4]], then A = B because they look the same." Is this reasoning sufficient for board exam marks? What must be explicitly stated?
questions.a: The reasoning is insufficient. For full marks, the student MUST explicitly state: (1) Both matrices have the same order (2 × 2), AND (2) each corresponding element is equal: a_11 = b_11 = 1, a_12 = b_12 = 2, a_21 = b_21 = 3, a_22 = b_22 = 4. Just saying "they look the same" gets 0 marks in CBSE. This tests whether the student knows the formal two-part definition of matrix equality.

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario (different from marks or inventory) where a 3 × 2 matrix naturally arises. Define what the rows and columns represent, and give a plausible numerical example.
questions.a: Example: A small café sells 3 items (coffee, tea, sandwich) over 2 days (Monday, Tuesday). Rows = items, Columns = days. Matrix = [[50, 60], [40, 45], [30, 35]] where entry (i,j) = quantity of item i sold on day j. A poor answer uses rows/columns interchangeably without definition, or creates a scenario that forces a 2×3 matrix instead (e.g., 2 items over 3 days), showing the student cannot distinguish row vs column meaning.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A matrix is an ordered ______ array of numbers or functions arranged in rows and columns, denoted by a capital letter.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are the class monitor and need to ______ the marks of 40 students in 5 subjects.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify the order of any given matrix, classify it into the correct type (row, column, square, diagonal, scalar, identity, zero), and determine whether two matrices are equal by comparing their orders and corresponding elements.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you are the class monitor and need to record the marks of 40 students in 5 ______.
